title: Dove Candle Ledgers
subject: Civil Procedure
stem:
Mary sued Peter in federal district court over a private contract for dove-shaped Christmas Eve candles sold through Peter’s “Light of the World” craft booth. During discovery, the judge ordered Peter to produce nonprivileged wax-batch logs, shipping receipts, and supplier invoices stored in a rented warehouse. Peter says paying workers to locate, box, and scan the papers will be expensive, so he seeks an immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine.

Call: Is the court of appeals likely to hear the appeal now?
call: Is the court of appeals likely to hear the appeal now?

choices.A: Yes, because any discovery order that deals with a side issue instead of the merits is immediately appealable.
choices.B: No, because an ordinary document-production order usually must wait for final-judgment review.
choices.C: No, because a discovery order can never be challenged by any route.
choices.D: Yes, because an expensive production order automatically qualifies as a collateral order.

rightExplanation:
B is the best answer. The order is an ordinary document-production order. The fact that retrieving and scanning the documents will cost money does not make the order immediately appealable.

Gold Key: Collateral-order review is narrow. A discovery order must fit the small class of orders that are effectively unreviewable after final judgment; ordinary discovery-cost complaints do not.

Silver Key: In an appealability array, read the fight as review now vs review later. Cut the extreme “any/every/never/automatically” answers first, then ask whether final-judgment review is enough.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: “automatically” is the overclaim. Expense does not automatically create immediate appeal.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: “never” is the overclaim. Waiting for final judgment is not the same as no challenge ever.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: one true-sounding prong is incomplete. “Side issue” / separate from merits is not enough.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: B. Ordinary document-production orders generally wait for final-judgment review.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: Not needed after the anchor-assisted CUT leaves one.

studentScript: Call: appeal now? Trigger: ordinary nonprivileged discovery plus expense. Cut any/never/automatically. Use the Gold Key: ordinary discovery waits. Pick B.

A.signal: The answer gives only side-issue separateness and treats it as enough.
A.lawyer: Collateral order doctrine also requires conclusiveness, importance, and effective unreviewability after final judgment.

B.signal: The answer matches the procedural gate and the ordinary-discovery trigger.
B.lawyer: Ordinary discovery orders generally do not qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine.

C.signal: The word never overclaims. Later or extraordinary review is not the same as immediate appeal.
C.lawyer: Discovery orders can be reviewed after final judgment or through extraordinary mechanisms in rare cases.

D.signal: Automatically turns litigation cost into immediate appeal.
D.lawyer: Cost and inconvenience do not make ordinary discovery orders collateral orders.

goldKeys.statement: Collateral-order review is narrow. Ordinary discovery orders generally wait for final judgment; expense alone is not effective unreviewability.
goldKeys.trigger: Immediate appeal from a discovery order under the collateral order doctrine.
